lines: IELTS Listening. The test is in four parts. Write all your answers in the listening question
booklet. At the end of the test, you'll be given ten minutes to transfer your answers
to an answer sheet. Now turned to part one, on page two of your question booklet.
Part one. You will hear a conversation between a man enrolling at a medical center and
receptionist. First you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen
carefully and answer questions one to six. Good morning sir how can I help you?
Hello there. Well I've just moved to this city and so I'd like to register as a
new patient here. Sure I'll just get the right form. Now first could I have a
name please? Yes my first name is Henry my middle name
as Ian, and the family name is Prestony. P-R-E-S-T-N-E-Y.
Right. And a date of birth?
It's the 17th of March, 1965.
Great. And your address, please?
52. Oh no, that was my old house. My address here is number 34, Market Road.
Right. Could I have your home number, sir?
Um, let me remember it. I haven't learned it yet. Two, eight, four. Sorry. Two, nine,
three, eight, four, seven, six. Yes, that's it. I've just had the phone connected.
Alrighty. Well, that's the contact details finished. Now, I need some other bits of information,
if you don't mind. First, I need to ask you which ethnic group do you most identify
with out of New Zealand Māori, Cook Island Māori, European, Tongan or Samoan.
European?
Right, thanks. That's just for statistical purposes. You know, we have to gather that info for the Ministry of Health.
And are you a New Zealand citizen?
Yes, I am.
Alright, I'll put that down. That's good. So you qualify for subsidised health care.
And now, do you hold any special cards such as a high user card or a low income card?
Yes, actually, I am a high user. I've had a lot of trouble with my back over the last 10 years.
Fine. I'll write that down for our records here so that you'll get that discount.
Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.
Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10.
And now, so that we can apply to have your medical records transferred here, can you tell
me the name of your previous health centre?
Yes, it was called Castle Hill.
Okay, I haven't heard of that practice before, so it can't be on Stewart Island or I'd
know it. And you don't sound like a Southlander anyway. So is it the North Island you've
come from?
Yes, you're quite right.
Okay. Well, I'll get you to sign this release form here, which gives us permission
to request the transfer of your file and then I can write to them and have your record sent to us.
Thank you. That'll be good.
Yes. It only takes a week or so to arrive usually.
Now, let's think about a doctor for you.
There are six doctors at the centre, so you have a choice.
Do you want to enrol with any particular one of them?
Well, no, not really. Being you here, I don't know any of them,
so it doesn't really matter.
I'd rather not have a female doctor though, if that's possible.
That's fine. I'll put down mail. That gives you three options, but some of those doctors only work part-time hours here, so would that be okay with you?
Oh, I see. Well, since I do have a chronic problem, which is why I hold the card we were talking about earlier, I would prefer seeing someone who'd not be hard to get hold of at any time.
So, you want a full-time doctor? I'll write that here. That is no problem, sir. Any other preferences?
Yes. My back is actually an old injury from playing rugby, so I'd like to see a sports specialist, if possible.
Well, let's see. I'll assign you to Dr Chang because he specialises in that branch of medicine.
Well, welcome to Dunedin, Mr Presney.
Thank you very much for all your help. You've been most kind.
That is the end of part one. You now have one minute to check your answers to part one.
Part 2 You'll hear the director of a children's club
talking to parents about the club's programmes. First you have some time to look at questions
11-14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11-14.
Good afternoon everyone. Thank you for coming. I'm the programme director here and I'll
begin by giving a little history about our after-school club and then I'll talk about
our summer camps. When we started the club in 1975 we didn't really have any set programs.
In the early 1980s several mothers and fathers wondered if we could add more programs so
we gave our approval and people from the community offered to help for free.
We've a variety of summer programs and they're very popular. Parents are pleased to send
their children here as we have great facilities and it gets their children away from the computer.
For the children they really appreciate the fact that the program is run by young staff
so it feels very different to school and they end up telling all their friends and bringing
them along too. In my position as director I love my work, despite how challenging it
is, I enjoy creating programmes for the children and although it's time consuming, it's very
rewarding to work out what we can do with the limited amount of income we receive. However,
finding committed people to fill the permanent positions here is a constant struggle. So
So if you know of anyone suitable please tell us.
We employ students to work part time in the summer.
They are usually in their last year of high school so need a bit of training.
We want them to be able to give guidance to any children who are homesick for example
so they attend a series of workshops to learn how to do that.
during the summer programme they work together to lead children in different activities and
on special occasions when there are outings to the zoo or local museums they are asked
to assist the trip director. Our summer programmes are popular and spaces
fill up really quickly. Registration opens on May 1st so to ensure that your child gets
into the one you want, we recommend you fill in the form on our website.
If you want to stop by our office, the staff can also answer your questions about the application
and our fees. Just be aware that applications for the summer
programmes have to be completed by mid-June. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you
have some time to look at questions 15-20. Now listen and answer questions 15-20.
During the summer holidays, we also offer various summer camps. These are held at different
places and last from a day to a week. At the beginning of the summer, we offer Elm camp.
Each morning, children go on a different walking trail in the forest to a nearby lake. Our
guides show them how to identify which wild mushrooms and berries are safe for eating.
feeding. In the evenings the groups also like to watch for deer feeding at the other side
of the lake. Maple camp is great for horse lovers. Mornings
are spent on a nearby farm and children participate in feeding the horses and brushing them down.
Each day includes an energetic ride through the fields. In the afternoons the kids
can either watch films or do some crafts. Willow Camp's got something for everyone.
There's painting, drawing and Latin dancing to salsa music. And anybody's chefs get
to work on their culinary skills as staff show them how to prepare healthy lunches
and bake fun snacks.
Cedar Camp will suit any aspiring rock stars.
In the morning they are part of a band and practice with pianos, guitars and drums.
They also learn about the recording process.
In the afternoon they perform for our younger campers.
Evenings there are always fun as students watch comedy and dramatic performances put
on by camp staff. Birch camp is a day camp, and all the food is provided. Children who
want to become authors love this one. They have classes in the morning with a children's
author. Then, in the afternoon, they put it all into practice by writing a short play.
There's a small lake here and the day often ends with a night swim under the stars.
At Pine Camp children get the chance to dress up as their favourite musician and sing a popular
song in front of a camera. They learn about the whole production process and, even better,
it's something they can show their families when they get home. Some even post their
movies online. Our evening barbecues there are always a hit with campers. If you're interested
in any more information, then please…
That is the end of part 2. You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to part 2.
Part 3. You will hear a conversation between an art history student called Terence and his
tutor about the student's plan for a class presentation.
First you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer
questions 21 to 24.
Okay Terence, now I've looked through your preliminary outline and notes for the presentation
on the art of the Efe region in Africa.
That's in Nigeria, right?
Yes. I'm concentrating on Efe sculptures from the 12th to the 15th century.
How did you get interested in that?
I know there have been some recent articles in the journals about African sculpture.
Well, I've read most of those now.
But initially I got my introduction to this at a special display at the City Museum a few years ago.
I just happened to be there and saw these works and saw they were fantastic.
And I even went to Nigeria last summer to see more of them.
I've seen the photos for your presentation and I must say the sculptures are gorgeous
portrayals of what appear to be kings and queens.
Yes.
I decided to concentrate on those as they're the most typical.
They're interesting because they're so naturalistic.
unlike the abstract figures we often associate with African art there's also a
lovely sculpture of a mudfish and one of the scaly crocodile but I didn't get
very good pictures of those so I won't spend long on them right so what was the
city of if a like when these works were made it's on the Niger River isn't it
yeah the boat traffic's what made it a center of commerce then as it still is
today, but nowadays it's better known as the home of a big university.
Speaking of modern day, Ife, tell me about your trip.
I was incredibly lucky to be able to get enough money to go.
My parents encouraged me, but they couldn't afford to send me.
I applied for a grant from the Arts Council, and in the end I got it.
I also wrote a series of articles about my trip for the local newspaper, but I didn't
get any money for that.
I was just pleased to get them published.
And the highlight of the trip?
That had to be meeting a professor working on the site in Ife,
who had been a young boy when they first discovered the sculptures by accident
at a building site in 1938.
He had been working at the site.
Of course, I also got to talk to lots of artists who were working there today
and I got to try my hand at making a little sculpture myself.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion,
Well, let's see what you might do to improve what you're planning for your presentation.
About the sculptures themselves, I think I need to add as much as possible about the
details of the way they were made. Of course, I can't add anything about the artists who
made them, because nobody really knows anything about them.
All good points, and you've certainly said enough about what the sculptures depict,
what the subjects are, that's well covered, but I'd make some bigger photos of them so you can clearly see the fine detail.
Okay.
And I would limit my personal reactions to these works of art if I were you. I know you think they're fantastic.
You're right. I'll contain my enthusiasm.
What about the section of the presentation which I call history?
I'd like to go into more depth about the history of that whole area, you know, in the countries around Nigeria.
That would make the presentation stronger.
But I think you've covered the situation regarding the rulers of the country quite well,
and you've got plenty already about what the Ife people were doing then and the way their society was structured.
And in fact, I think you could cut out the bit about modern Nigerian history because it's not relevant.
I agree. That doesn't fit. But perhaps I should concentrate more on the religious beliefs,
since all these sculptures do seem to have some kind of religious association.
Good. I can lend you a book on that.
Now, probably the part the class will find most interesting is the report of your trip to Nigeria
and the research you did there. So I gather you managed to use the University
Library in Ife. Yes. As soon as I'd explained why I wanted the information,
that was no problem. They couldn't have been more helpful. There were some
interesting accounts of how the first sculptures were found and what happened
to them, which I want to include. What struck me when I saw the sculptures in
Nigeria is the extent to which 20th century European artists were
influenced by them. But that's beyond the scope of my presentation, I think.
Yes. What about the sources of the materials they used? You don't mention that anywhere.
I didn't manage to find out much about that. I want to cover the theories about who the
original sculptors were, though. Yes, the idea that a lot of them may have
been made by the same person. That's very interesting.
It is, isn't it? Right. Well, thanks for all the advice.
That is the end of Part 3.
You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to Part 3.
Part 4 You will hear part of a geography lecture about
rubber production. First, you have some time to look at questions
31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good morning. In this module we've been looking at the production of some of the world's most
important raw materials, and today it's the turn of rubber. Traditionally, natural
rubber was produced on small holdings, and in case you're not familiar with the
process, I'll just describe it briefly. The first stage in the process, known as
tapping, involves making an incision in the rubber tree and removing a thin layer
of bark. This procedure has to be done very carefully with a special knife,
because if the incision is too deep, the tree will be damaged. And a white
liquid known as latex starts to ooze out.
Next, the tapper attaches a cup to the tree, made out of something simple like a coconut
shell to collect it.
Tapping is usually started in the early morning, because the coolness encourages the latex
to flow easily.
Later in the day, the tapper goes back to each tree to get the latex, and take it
to what you might call the factory, although the procedures that take place in it are
relatively simple. Here it is poured into a mold and then formic acid is added to
it and the mixtures left for a few hours. The purpose of the formic acid is to
thicken the liquid latex. So after some time the latex is transformed into a
solid block of rubber. This block of rubber is then pressed manually to turn
it into a thin sheet.
And then, when it's thin enough, the rubber sheet is fed through a mangle.
And I should point out that apart from this, no other machinery is used in the process.
It's fairly simple, just a frame with two rollers and a handle to turn them.
The procedure is repeated several times to get rid of as much water as possible.
And finally, these sheets are taken to a special smoke room where they are dried.
And you're then left with, what are by now, sheets of brown rubber.
These are then sold to traders, who collect them from villages and sell them on in turn.
Well, that's the process then.
Now just a little bit about the history of rubber.
Rubber was in use in America long before it became commercially important.
The rubber tree was a native of Brazil and there's an account from as long ago as 1525 of people in
Mexico playing with rubber balls. But it wasn't until the 19th century that Europeans recognized
the usefulness of the substance chiefly for clothing. Various attempts were made to
improve the properties of rubber. One of the key discoveries was of a process known
as vulcanization, which involved heating the rubber and adding sulfur to it.
And the result was a substance that had a lot more strength and was also more elastic, making
it suitable for a variety of uses.
But the thing that gave demand for rubber a real boost was the expanding automobile
industry at the end of the 19th century and the invention of car tires.
During the 20th century, rubber became so important that there were various attempts to develop a synthetic version.
But none of them resulted in a product that was able to compete with natural rubber
until Germany developed a successful substitute when its supplies of the natural substance were cut off during the First World War.
Later, this was accelerated when the American government built its own rubber factories.
So, in economic terms, Rubber's had an outstanding position in the global market for more than
a hundred years.
That is the end of part four.
You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
That is the end of the listening test.
You now have ten minutes to transfer your answers to the listening answer sheet.
You have two minutes left.
You have one minute left.
Please stop writing and wait for your question booklet to be collected.
